Deep time · still alive

Older than
the written word.

Scroll back through everything humans have ever done — the Moon landing, Rome, the pyramids, the first sentence ever written — and keep going. These seven living things were already ancient before any of it. Every one is alive right now, as you read this.

Begin the descent
57 yrs ago The first human footprints are pressed into the Moon.
~2,000 yrs Rome rules the Mediterranean world.
A cushion in the driest desert

La Llareta

Azorella compacta
3,000+years old

It looks like green paint poured over the rocks and left to harden. It is neither moss nor stone — it's a flowering shrub, a cousin of parsley, grown so tight and dense you could sit on it without leaving a mark.

It lives above 15,000 feet in a part of the Atacama with no rainfall in recorded history, adding less than a millimeter to itself each year.

Atacama Desert, Chile
The world thenStonehenge was already old, and Homer had not yet been born.
~4,600 yrs The last stones of the Great Pyramid are set at Giza.
The oldest tree that isn't a clone

Methuselah

Pinus longaeva · Great Basin bristlecone pine
4,850years old

Not a colony, not a root network — one continuous tree, the oldest single non-clonal organism known. Its precise location in California's White Mountains is kept secret to protect it.

Bristlecones endure by surrendering. Most of the trunk dies back over the centuries, and a thin ribbon of living bark carries the whole tree forward, one grudging cell at a time.

White Mountains, California
The world thenIt was already a young tree when the Pyramid was finished. Writing itself was a brand-new human invention.
~5,200 yrs The first words are written down, in Sumerian clay.
Life on the edge of the possible

Antarctic Moss

Moss bank · Elephant Island
5,500years old

A single bank of moss on a rock in one of the least hospitable places on Earth. It grows perhaps a hundredth of an inch a year, only in the few weeks of Antarctic summer when the ice loosens its grip.

Scientists study it the way they study trees — by coring down through the living surface into millennia of its own compressed past.

Elephant Island, Antarctica
The world thenOlder than the wheel. Older than the first city walls.
A young tree on ancient roots

Old Tjikko

Picea abies · Norway spruce
9,560years old

Above ground it's an unremarkable spruce, a few feet tall and only a few centuries old. The wonder is beneath it: a root system carbon-dated to nearly ten thousand years, sending up a fresh trunk each time the last one dies.

The tree you would see is only the newest in an unbroken line the same organism has grown since the ice withdrew.

Fulufjället, Sweden
The world thenIts roots first took hold as the last Ice Age released Scandinavia and agriculture was just being invented.
~11,700 yrs The last Ice Age ends. Farming begins.
A forest that is one tree

Pando

Populus tremuloides · quaking aspen
~14,000years old (est.)

47,000 trunks across 106 acres — all one organism, genetically identical, fed by a single root system. Each "tree" is only a stem. Together they weigh some 13 million pounds, the heaviest living thing ever measured.

Its true age is genuinely uncertain: many thousands of years at the least, and by some estimates far, far more.

Fishlake National Forest, Utah
The world thenIf the higher estimates hold, Pando was already spreading when mammoths still walked North America.
~40,000 yrs Humans paint the first animals on cave walls.
A meadow beneath the sea

Posidonia Seagrass

Posidonia oceanica
100,000years old

A single meadow of seagrass stretching for miles across the Mediterranean floor, quietly cloning itself sideways for a thousand centuries in the protected water between Ibiza and Formentera.

It is one of the oldest living things on the planet, and almost no one who swims above it knows it is there.

Balearic Islands, Spain
The world thenIt began before our species left Africa — when the only humans in Europe were Neanderthals.
~300,000 yrs The first members of our species, Homo sapiens, appear.
The oldest, and the strangest

Siberian Actinobacteria

Living permafrost colony
500,000years old

The oldest living thing yet found — and it has not been asleep. Locked in frozen ground, in total dark, below freezing, this bacterial colony has been slowly repairing its own DNA for close to half a million years. Not dormant. Alive, in the fullest sense, just unimaginably slow.

It was found by scientists hunting for clues to what life might look like on other, colder worlds.

Siberian permafrost
The world thenIt predates our species entirely. When it began, there were no Homo sapiens anywhere on Earth.
You have reached the bottom

Half a million years down, and still breathing.

Every organism on this page is alive at this moment — not fossilized, not preserved, but living: growing, cloning, repairing, adding its fraction of a millimeter. They were here before the pyramids, before writing, before us. They keep no record and ask for nothing. They simply continue.

We measure our lives in decades and our history in a few thousand years, and it feels like a lot. Then you meet the moss.

Next time a week feels long — remember the bacteria that spent five hundred thousand years mending itself in the dark, and just kept going.

About the numbers

The ages here are drawn from published science and from Rachel Sussman's decade-long project The Oldest Living Things in the World. Clonal organisms — Pando, Old Tjikko, the seagrass, the moss — are dated by their root or genetic continuity, not a single trunk, and several of these ages are estimates that remain debated; Pando's especially spans a wide range. The bristlecone Methuselah is the oldest verified non-clonal individual. The depth instrument in the corner is logarithmic and approximate — it exists to convey scale, not a precise reading.
